title: Heavy bleeding pressure-and-handover routine
content: Extreme bleeding needs immediate pressure, calm role assignment, and fast professional escalation. The guide records times and actions without turning untrained people into surgeons.
steps: Use direct pressure with the cleanest available cloth or dressing.
Keep pressure steady and send someone for emergency help.
Do not repeatedly lift the dressing to look.
If trained and locally allowed, use bleeding-control equipment according to training only.
Record start time, visible blood loss, and changes.

title: Severed body part preservation boundary
content: For amputation-type injuries, the priority is the living person: bleeding control, shock prevention, urgent transport, and clean handling of the separated part without unsafe experiments.
steps: Care for the person first, especially bleeding and warmth.
Place the separated part in the cleanest available bag or wrapping.
Keep it cool if safe, but avoid direct contact with ice or dirty water.
Label time and identity.
Send it with the person to professional care.

title: Crush injury release warning card
content: After long entrapment under rubble, sudden release can be medically dangerous. The entry focuses on urgent rescue coordination, time records, warmth, and rapid professional care.
steps: Record how long the person may have been trapped.
Do not pull or lift debris unsafely; protect rescuers too.
Call professional rescue and medical help as early as possible.
Keep the person warm, calm, and still if safe.
Report crushed limb, dark urine, severe pain, weakness, or confusion urgently.

title: Impaled object do-not-pull rule
content: An object stuck in the body can be blocking bleeding. This entry prevents the common deadly mistake of pulling it out without trained care.
steps: Do not remove the object unless it blocks breathing and trained help says so.
Stabilize around it with bulky clean material.
Control bleeding around the injury without pressing the object deeper.
Keep the person still and warm.
Arrange urgent transport and write the time.

title: Open chest injury emergency escalation
content: Chest trauma with breathing trouble is a high-risk emergency. The goal is calm positioning, minimal handling, urgent care, and clear handover.
steps: Call emergency help immediately.
Let the person find the easiest breathing position unless spinal injury is suspected.
Cover obvious open wounds with the cleanest available material without pushing inside.
Watch breathing, skin color, consciousness, and worsening pain.
Prepare rapid handover.

title: Abdominal injury protection and no-food rule
content: Severe abdominal trauma can worsen with movement, food, drink, or pressure. This entry keeps the person still, protected, and ready for urgent care.
steps: Call emergency help
Do not give food, alcohol, or unnecessary medicine.
Cover exposed tissue with the cleanest moist clean barrier if trained supplies are available; do not push anything back inside.
Keep knees slightly supported if comfortable and trauma allows.
Watch for shock, worsening pain, pale skin, or confusion.

title: Open fracture contamination control
content: An open fracture is a major infection and bleeding risk. The entry focuses on covering, immobilizing without force, and urgent evacuation.
steps: Call for urgent care.
Do not push bone or tissue back in.
Cover with the cleanest available dressing.
Immobilize the limb in the position found if possible.
Check color, warmth, feeling, and movement beyond the injury without forcing.

title: Pelvic injury minimal movement rule
content: Falls, crushes, and vehicle impacts can hide pelvic bleeding. This entry prevents unnecessary movement and flags rapid evacuation.
steps: Suspect pelvic injury after major force, fall, crush, or severe hip/groin pain.
Do not repeatedly roll, sit, or walk the person.
Keep them still and warm.
Track pulse, alertness, skin color, and pain changes.
Get professional help for transport.

title: Blast injury hidden damage watch
content: Blast survivors may look okay while hearing, lungs, abdomen, or brain injury worsens later. The entry creates a delayed-symptom watch list.
steps: Move away from secondary hazards first.
Record distance from blast, time, and protection used.
Watch for breathing trouble, chest pain, abdominal pain, vomiting, confusion, hearing loss, severe headache, or bleeding.
Keep the person under observation even if they can walk.
Send urgent cases to professional care first.
